damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - Ministry hearing; Dumbledore arrives and departs without acknowledging Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes that Harry feels a powerful, fortifying emotion at seeing Dumbledore ('a fortified, hopeful feeling rather like that which phoenix song gave him') and desperately wants to catch Dumbledore's eye throughout the hearing. Dumbledore's deliberate avoidance is a conscious, painful choice driven by his fear of Voldemort exploiting their connection. After the acquittal, Dumbledore departs 'without looking once at Harry', and Harry later reflects with hurt that Dumbledore had visited Grimmauld Place without asking to see him. This behaviour is part of a sustained, explained pattern of protective distance.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film condenses the hearing to a brisk procedural scene (Film Scene 2-3). Dumbledore arrives, intercedes competently, and the moment of his ignoring Harry is not dramatised as a felt wound. There is no internal Harry reaction registering the hurt of being unseen, no 'without looking once at Harry' beat given weight. The film presents Dumbledore's competence without the accompanying emotional cost to Harry of being deliberately blanked by the one person he most wants to turn to.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses the hearing to establish both Dumbledore's brilliance and the painful asymmetry of his relationship with Harry at this point: Harry gains legal safety but loses emotional contact. The film captures the first without the second, flattening a key relationship beat that motivates Harry's growing resentment toward Dumbledore across the whole fifth year.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - Dumbledore's office post-battle; Harry wrecks the office (cut scene)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book devotes a long, climactic scene to Harry's grief-rage after Sirius's death: he destroys instruments in Dumbledore's office, screams, demands to be let out, and Dumbledore calmly absorbs it all without flinching, ultimately saying 'I daresay I have too many' possessions. This is the emotional climax of the book's Dumbledore arc — he accepts Harry's fury as deserved, takes full responsibility for Sirius's death, explains years of withholding, and weeps. It is the scene in which their relationship is fundamentally renegotiated.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene is listed in the non-theatrical exclusions as cut from the theatrical release. The film replaces it with a brief exchange (Film Scene 10) in which Dumbledore says 'the fault is mine' and explains he distanced himself to protect Harry, and Harry says 'I care too much about you.' There is no destroyed office, no screaming, no prolonged confrontation, no Dumbledore absorbing Harry's physical rage, no extended confession of old-man mistakes, no prophecy explanation delivered in full dramatic context.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the single most damaging absence in the adaptation. The office-wrecking scene is the structural and emotional climax of Dumbledore's arc in Book 5: it is where he takes moral responsibility, explains his failures, reveals the prophecy, and demonstrates that he loves Harry enough to let Harry rage at him. Removing it means the audience never sees Dumbledore's full confession, never sees him weep, never experiences the cathartic renegotiation of the relationship. The replacement exchange is too short and too calm to carry this weight. The saga-level theme — that Dumbledore's greatest flaw is loving Harry so much he withheld truth — is severely compressed and loses most of its emotional power.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - Grimmauld Place kitchen; Dumbledore's absence from Harry's hearing night visit
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 141 establishes that Dumbledore visited Grimmauld Place the night before Harry's hearing and did not ask to see him. 'The thought that Dumbledore had been in the house on the eve of his hearing and not asked to see him made him feel, if it were possible, even worse.' This compounds Harry's sense of abandonment and feeds his growing resentment toward Dumbledore as a deliberate, ongoing pattern.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film does not include this beat. There is no moment where Harry learns Dumbledore was nearby and chose not to see him. The cumulative texture of Dumbledore's deliberate distancing — which in the book builds across multiple small moments — is largely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While individually small, this beat contributes to the book's careful construction of Harry's alienation from Dumbledore. Its absence means the film's Harry has less justified grievance, weakening the emotional credibility of his resentment and making Dumbledore's later apology feel less earned.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - Dumbledore's Army confrontation in Dumbledore's office; Dumbledore takes blame
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 609-652 show Dumbledore engineering an elaborate, witty escape from arrest while protecting Harry: he claims the DA was his idea, outmanoeuvres Fudge and two Aurors, and flees via Fawkes — all while giving Harry last urgent instructions about Occlumency. The scene showcases his strategic brilliance, courage, self-sacrifice, and dry humour ('I could break out, of course — but what a waste of time'). He also privately thanks Kingsley for the memory modification.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 5 includes this sequence and largely preserves it: Dumbledore takes responsibility, delivers the 'come quietly' line, and departs stylishly. The film does capture the essence of Dumbledore's agency and wit here. This is a relatively faithful moment.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film mostly preserves this scene. Minor compression removes some of the book's extended wit (the 'waste of time breaking out' line, the private aside to McGonagall about Kingsley), slightly reducing the texture of Dumbledore's voice, but damage is minimal. Scored low accordingly.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - Ministry Atrium duel with Voldemort
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 725-783 show Dumbledore duelling Voldemort with extraordinary controlled power and philosophical calm: he speaks about the nature of death and love mid-combat ('there are things much worse than death'), refuses to kill, and after Voldemort attempts to possess Harry, Dumbledore's response is to call 'Stay where you are, Harry!' with genuine fear in his voice — the only time he sounds frightened. He then calmly takes charge of the aftermath, issuing Fudge orders and arranging Harry's return.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 9 depicts the duel but compresses the philosophical dialogue significantly. The line 'It was foolish of you to come here tonight, Tom. The Orders are on their way' and Dumbledore's post-duel authority over Fudge are present. However, the extended philosophical exchange about death ('There is nothing worse than death, Dumbledore!' / 'You are quite wrong') is stripped to a minimal exchange. The nuanced portrait of Dumbledore as someone who fights without seeking to kill, and whose deepest weapon is understanding love and death better than Voldemort, is thinned.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The duel is the one moment in Book 5 where Dumbledore's philosophy becomes action. The dialogue mid-duel establishes the thematic core of the entire saga: Voldemort's inability to understand love is his fatal weakness. Stripping this reduces Dumbledore from a philosopher-warrior to a technically impressive duelist, weakening the saga-level thematic payoff.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - Throughout film; Dumbledore's deliberate avoidance of Harry presented without accumulated texture
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book builds Dumbledore's avoidance of Harry across dozens of small moments: not looking at him at the hearing, not visiting him in Grimmauld Place, Snape being assigned Occlumency instead of Dumbledore himself, Harry noticing Dumbledore seems to look just over his shoulder rather than at him, etc. (Book Scenes 141, 193, 196, 272, 301, 411-417, 465-466, 492). This accumulation is essential: it makes Harry's resentment fully understandable and makes Dumbledore's later explanation and apology feel proportionate to a year of real abandonment.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film acknowledges the distance in dialogue (Film Scene 10: 'I thought by distancing myself from you... he'd be less tempted') but does not dramatise it through accumulated small moments. There is no scene where Harry registers the specific pain of being not-looked-at. The explanation is delivered but the behaviour it explains has not been sufficiently shown.
damaging_scenes.explanation: When the film's Dumbledore explains that he distanced himself all year, the audience has not felt that distance accumulate the way book readers have. The apology and explanation therefore land with less emotional weight. This undermines one of the book's central arcs: that Dumbledore's protective love manifested as a year of painful abandonment, and that this was a genuine mistake with genuine consequences.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - Post-battle Dumbledore's office (Film Scene 10, theatrical cut replacement)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book's extended office scene includes Dumbledore explicitly taking responsibility: 'It is my fault that Sirius died... almost entirely my fault.' He explains each decision error in detail — not teaching Occlumency himself, not telling Harry the prophecy sooner, allowing Snape's lessons to continue despite knowing the tension. He also reveals the prophecy in full, with the Pensieve, giving context to everything Harry has endured. Finally, he mentions he deliberately did not make Harry a prefect because he had 'enough responsibility to be going on with', and is seen with a tear on his face.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 10 (the replacement scene, which per the exclusion note is the post-Sirius office exchange that replaced the book's scene) gives Dumbledore: 'No, the fault is mine... I thought by distancing myself from you... I care too much about you.' Harry responds: 'Why didn't you tell me?' The prophecy is delivered not by Dumbledore in the office but as a discovered recording in the Department of Mysteries (Film Scene 7). The full moral accounting — Dumbledore cataloguing his specific failures — is gone.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film's replacement condenses Dumbledore's confession to two sentences. The book's version is a sustained, unflinching self-examination by the most powerful wizard in the world, admitting that he let a boy suffer for years out of a misguided protective love. This is Dumbledore's defining moral moment in the entire series and the foundation for understanding his character in Books 6 and 7. The compression means the film Dumbledore never truly reckons with his failures at the granular level the books establish, reducing his characterisation from tragically flawed mentor to merely a kind old man who made one tactical error.

main_damage_causes: The theatrical cut of the office-wrecking scene removes the emotional and moral climax of Dumbledore's entire Book 5 arc — his full confession, self-recrimination, and renegotiation of his relationship with Harry — leaving the film's Dumbledore without a defining moment of moral accountability.

The accumulated texture of Dumbledore's deliberate avoidance of Harry across the film year is not dramatised sufficiently, meaning the film's abbreviated explanation ('I distanced myself to protect you') describes behaviour the audience has not fully felt, robbing the apology of its proportionate emotional weight.

The duel with Voldemort strips the philosophical dialogue that establishes Dumbledore as a thinker-warrior whose deepest understanding — that love is more powerful than death — is the saga's central theme, reducing him to a technically impressive but philosophically silent combatant.
